newsitem.title: AZERBAIJAN: Azerbaijan's own oil exports locked in pipeline row.
newsitem.headline: Azerbaijan's own oil exports locked in pipeline row.

text.p: Azerbaijan's state oil sector, determined to find its own place in markets and not be overshadowed by its big foreign energy partners in the Caspian, faces a struggle to export oil, energy sources said on Thursday.
Azerbaijan has an agreement with Moscow to send some crude produced by its joint ventures through Russia's sprawling oil export pipeline system to Novorossiisk, on the Black Sea.
The former Soviet republic also wants access to the pipeline for its own oil not produced by joint ventures.
But officials at Azeri state oil company SOCAR said Russia is locking it out of the former Soviet Union's pipeline system, which is still mostly run by Moscow.
The Azeri-Russian intergovernmental agreement is to send Azeri joint venture oil via Russia's 1,300 km (800 mile) pipeline from the Azeri capital Baku to Novorossisk.
The agreement includes a clause specifying that SOCAR oil would be sent via the link as a test run for future shipments of Azeri joint venture oil, due to come on stream in August.
But a SOCAR official, who declined to be identified, said Transneft, the Russian pipeline monopoly, had said the agreement covered only oil produced by joint ventures, and not SOCAR oil.
"We were very surprised," the official said. "The agreement which we both signed is in relation to Azeri oil.
"It is not important who actually produces the oil or who the owner is."
But it is important for Moscow, which is smarting at its loss of control over oil production in the former Soviet Union and racing to influence the flow of all oil from the region.
SOCAR was due to send a test load of 70,000 tonnes of its own output via the link as a trial run for the AIOC oil.

But it says Transneft has delayed the test run -- officially, due to questions over the role of the war-torn Chechen capital Grozny, through which the pipeline runs, and unofficially, to show Baku that Moscow controls the flow of the region's natural resources.
A Transneft spokesman said Moscow would honour its shipment agreement with the Baku.
But the SOCAR official said Transneft had brought up the question of higher transit fees for SOCAR oil -- a matter which SOCAR views as aimed at keeping Baku off of world oil markets.

Azerbaijan's biggest oil investor, the 13-member Azerbaijan International Operating Company (AIOC), led by British Petroleum Plc and Statoil of Norway, will use the main Russian pipeline to send its early oil from August to markets.
SOCAR First Deputy Director Sayat Ibragimov said SOCAR President Natik Aliyev and AIOC President Terry Adams would visit Moscow for talks with Transneft on March 24.
SOCAR wanted to agree a timetable for moving the SOCAR oil, while AIOC wanted assurances that the pipeline would be ready in August to handle its joint venture output as planned, he said.

But SOCAR is still worried about how it will export its own future output. Azeri crude has not been exported in significant amounts to world markets since the republic was swallowed up in 1920 by the Soviet empire.

That has spurred SOCAR to seek alternative export routes, and the Azeri government has a deal with former Soviet republic Georgia to export 500,000 tonnes of SOCAR output over an unspecified period via railroad to Georgian Black Sea ports.
The agreement has already sent 10,000 tonnes via Georgia.
SOCAR estimates its oil exports will total just 10 percent of its total output of around 190,000 barrels per day in 1997.
That is a fraction of output joint ventures will have in coming years -- but SOCAR officials said that Baku still wanted its own place in world markets.
